analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2010 estate tax cuts permanent instead of letting them expire.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; with only its sponsor and two cosponsors, it died in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2010 tax law cut the federal estate tax — set the exemption at $5 million per person ($10 million per married couple) with a 35% top rate — but only through the end of 2012, after which pre-2001 rules (a $1 million exemption and a 55% top rate) were scheduled to return. This bill would strike the expiration date and make the lower tax permanent. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $5 million per person ($10 million per couple). Permanent extension would spare those estates from the scheduled reversion to the $1 million exemption and 55% top rate after 2012. A small number of very large estates pay the estate tax, so the benefit is heavily concentrated at the top of the wealth distribution.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would permanently extend the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax revisions enacted in the Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010, which had been scheduled to expire at the end of 2012 [S2].

In practical terms, that means keeping the 2010 law's large exemption and low top rate — roughly $5 million per person and a 35% rate — instead of returning after 2012 to the pre-2001 estate tax, which taxed estates above $1 million at rates up to 55% [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, in the form of estate tax revenue never collected from the largest estates. That lost revenue would be made up through larger deficits or other taxes, spread across all taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Making the 2010 estate tax provisions permanent would give up estate tax revenue indefinitely; the 2010 law's expiration date existed specifically to limit that law's long-term cost [S3].
Only a small share of estates exceed the $5 million exemption, so the benefit of the bill would flow almost entirely to the wealthiest families, while the revenue cost is borne broadly [S3].

Supporters of stronger estate taxation argue the tax falls on large inherited wealth that would otherwise go untaxed; permanently cutting it shifts more of the tax load onto earnings and other sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the handful of families with estates above the exemption, permanence is worth a great deal. For everyone else, the bill offered no direct benefit and carried a real cost in foregone revenue. The tradeoff is lopsided toward a concentrated group.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote — before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Shelley Berkley introduced the bill on May 5, 2011 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
The bill drew two cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].
No further action was recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 2010 estate tax provisions remained temporary, keeping in place the scheduled reversion to a $1 million exemption and a 55% top rate unless Congress later acted. The federal treasury came out ahead relative to what permanent extension would have cost; no industry or interest group moved the bill, so no concentrated interest gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The treasury; no interest group gained

for.name: Rep. Shelley Berkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2010 estate tax provisions permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, an unusual pattern for an estate tax cut, but with only three backers and no recorded floor or committee votes, the partisan shape of the fight never took form.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates (households above $5 million)
industries.note: The bill would permanently spare estates above the 2010 law's exemption from higher tax, a direct transfer of foregone estate revenue to the wealthiest families. The cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone else.

industries.industry: Closely held family businesses and large farms
industries.note: Owners of larger family businesses and farms are the group most often cited as facing the estate tax; permanent extension of the higher exemption would reduce the risk heirs must sell assets to pay the tax. Most such operations, however, already fall under the exemption.
